match.reason: Neither bank point teaches how a business keeps its competitive advantage by innovating after rivals copy it: the first only defines competitive advantage at Year 9 depth, and the second covers entrepreneurs and innovation in general at a Year 11 NSW level, so a new point is needed.

draft.title: Keeping an advantage through entrepreneurship
card: An advantage does not last on its own. When a business does well with an idea, rivals can copy it, and the edge shrinks.
Innovating
bringing in a new product, service or way of working. A new idea gives the business something rivals do not yet have.
Improving products
making an existing product better over time, such as adding features or fixing faults, so customers keep choosing it over copies.
New markets
selling to new groups of customers or in new places, such as another city or country, where the business can grow and rivals may not yet compete.
draft.remember: Rivals copy, so entrepreneurs keep innovating, improving and finding new markets.

a.q: Why must a business keep innovating even after it wins customers with a successful idea?
opts: Rivals can copy the idea and shrink its edge
Customers always stop buying after a year
Innovation is the only way to cut costs
A successful idea can never be sold again
a.why: Rivals can copy a successful idea, so the edge it gave may shrink over time. Customers do not always stop buying, so the reason is the copying, not a fixed time limit.
a.clue: Think about what rivals do when they see an idea working.

b.q: Priya's bakery in Ballarat sells a popular sourdough loaf. A rival bakery starts selling a very similar loaf. Which response is an example of finding a new market?
opts: Selling her loaves at weekend markets in Geelong
Adding seeds to her loaf to improve the recipe
Launching a new gluten-free loaf in her own shop
Fixing the shop's oven so loaves bake evenly
b.why: Selling in Geelong reaches new customers in a new place. Adding seeds improves the existing product, and the gluten-free loaf is a new product, so those are different responses.
b.clue: Which choice is about where or to whom she sells, not what she bakes?

a.best: Rivals can copy the idea and shrink its edge

b.best: Selling her loaves at weekend markets in Geelong
also_right: Launching a new gluten-free loaf in her own shop

problems.detail: The question asks why a business 'must' keep innovating, but the card only says rivals 'can' copy an idea and businesses keep their edge by innovating.
Every wrong option uses an absolute word ('always', 'only', 'never'), and the right option is the only one with the card's 'can'. A student could pick it without knowing the idea.

The card defines new markets as 'selling to new groups of customers', and a gluten-free loaf reaches a new group (people who avoid gluten). This makes that option defensable as finding a new market. The clue's 'to whom she sells' strengthens this reading. Use a distractor that does not also reach new customers.

a.q: Why do businesses keep innovating after a successful idea has won them customers?
opts: Rivals can copy the idea, so its edge can shrink
Winning customers makes rival businesses leave
The government limits how long a product is sold
A popular product gets dearer to make each year
a.why: Rivals can copy an idea that is working, so the edge it gave can shrink, and new ideas restore it. Success does not drive rivals away: it tends to draw them in to copy.
a.clue: Think about what rivals do when they see an idea working.

b.q: Priya's bakery in Ballarat sells a popular sourdough loaf. A rival bakery starts selling a very similar loaf. Which response is an example of finding a new market?
opts: Selling her loaves at weekend markets in Geelong
Adding seeds to her sourdough to improve the recipe
Baking a new fruit loaf for her regular customers
Buying a new oven that bakes her loaves faster
b.why: Selling in Geelong takes her loaves to new customers in a new place. The fruit loaf is a new product, but it goes to the same regular customers, so it is innovating, not a new market. Adding seeds improves the existing product, and the oven is a new way of working.
b.clue: Which choice changes where she sells, not what or how she bakes?

a.best: Rivals can copy the idea, so its edge can shrink

b.best: Selling her loaves at weekend markets in Geelong
